ai-27.title: Latency waterfall: sequential versus parallel tools
ai-27.prompt: Compare this analytical schedule with spans from the separate local timing probe. Parallelize only when both tool calls are independent.

ai-28.title: SLO budget: keep the critical path inside the deadline
ai-28.prompt: Toy request budget: 800 ms. Retrieval takes 250 ms, two independent tools each take 240 ms, and generation takes 500 ms. Choose the execution policy, predict whether the end-to-end budget is met, then inspect the timing trace.
ai-28.controlPrompt: How should the two independent tool calls run?
ai-28.predictionPrompt: Will the request finish within its 800 ms budget?

options.label: Run both tools sequentially
options.context: Critical path = retrieval + tool A + tool B + generation.
options.result: 1,230 ms total · misses the 800 ms budget by 430 ms.
options.explanation: Sequential independent calls add both durations to the critical path. A request can have fast individual spans and still miss its end-to-end SLO.

options.label: Run both independent tools in parallel
options.context: Critical path = retrieval + max(tool A, tool B) + generation.
options.result: 990 ms total · misses the budget by 190 ms, even after parallelizing.
options.explanation: Parallelizing independent work shortens the critical path, but it cannot make a 990 ms path fit an 800 ms deadline. You still need a measured fallback or a smaller scope.

options.label: Parallel tools with a 300 ms generation cap
options.context: Return a concise answer with available evidence when the generation cap is reached.
options.result: 790 ms total · within budget, with a deliberately shorter response.
options.explanation: A budget is useful only when each stage respects a deadline and the system defines what to return when a stage is capped. This is an analytical toy schedule, not a latency guarantee.

ai-29.title: Retry policy: spend the deadline once
ai-29.prompt: A request has a 900 ms deadline. The provider attempt can take 500 ms, and a known-good cached response is available in 120 ms. Choose a policy and predict the user-visible outcome after a timeout.
ai-29.controlPrompt: What should the service do after the first attempt times out at 500 ms?
ai-29.predictionPrompt: What does the learner receive before the 900 ms deadline?

options.label: Retry without an attempt deadline
options.context: The retry may consume another 500 ms; no fallback is configured.

predictions.label: A late provider response or timeout

options.result: The retry outlives the request deadline; no timely response is available.
options.explanation: Retries consume the same user-facing budget unless a new deadline is explicitly defined. Unbounded retrying can turn a transient fault into a long outage.

options.label: One bounded attempt, then serve the cached response
options.context: Use the 500 ms attempt timeout; fallback takes 120 ms and carries its original evidence metadata.

predictions.label: A late provider response or timeout

options.result: The cached response returns in 620 ms and retains its evidence metadata.
options.explanation: A fallback is safe only when it is known-good, bounded, and honest about its freshness. Do not fabricate current citations from a stale cache.

options.label: One short retry, then cached response
options.context: The retry is capped at 180 ms; the cache fallback takes 120 ms.

predictions.label: A late provider response or timeout

options.result: The bounded retry fails, then a cached response returns at 800 ms.
options.explanation: A retry can be useful when its error class is retryable and enough time remains for a fallback. Use jitter and idempotency for real systems; these fixed durations are illustrative.

ai-30.title: Canary gate: an aggregate can hide a broken slice
ai-30.prompt: A candidate has 96% aggregate success, but a high-risk slice has only 70% success. The release policy requires 90% aggregate and 85% for every risk slice. Choose a promotion rule and predict the release action.
ai-30.controlPrompt: Which gate should the release controller use?
ai-30.predictionPrompt: Should this candidate receive more traffic?

options.label: Gate on aggregate success only
options.context: The aggregate is 96%; this rule ignores slice-level regressions.

transitions.label: Increase traffic
transitions.observation: Candidate receives the next traffic step

options.result: The aggregate-only rule promotes a candidate with a known risk-slice regression.
options.explanation: An aggregate can hide harm concentrated in a smaller cohort. A release gate should include the slices that matter to the product and policy.

options.label: Require aggregate and every risk slice to pass
options.context: Promote only if aggregate ≥ 90% and every listed risk slice ≥ 85%.

transitions.label: Hold traffic
transitions.observation: No promotion · assign owner to investigate

options.result: Promotion halts until the slice regression is understood and the gate passes.
options.explanation: A failed canary gate is evidence to stop and investigate. It does not alone prove the candidate caused the regression, so compare matched baselines before deciding whether to roll back.

options.label: Rollback on any failed risk slice
options.context: This policy rolls back once a statistically reviewed risk slice falls below its threshold.

transitions.label: Restore stable version
transitions.observation: Traffic returns to the last known-good version

options.result: The policy restores the stable version after the reviewed slice gate fails.
options.explanation: Automatic rollback is appropriate only when the signal is reliable, the threshold is predeclared, and rollback is safe. Otherwise halt traffic and investigate first.

ai-36.title: Provider failure: classify before you retry
ai-36.prompt: The provider returns either a transient timeout or a permanent invalid-credential error. A last-known-good response is available. Choose a recovery policy and predict how it handles each condition.
ai-36.controlPrompt: How should the service classify and recover from provider errors?
ai-36.predictionPrompt: What happens when the selected error occurs?

options.label: Retry every error twice
options.context: Both timeouts and invalid credentials consume two extra attempts.

predictions.label: Transient error may recover; permanent error stops early
Every error is guaranteed to recover

transitions.label: Retry attempt 1 and 2
transitions.observation: Same credential is reused; both calls fail

transitions.label: Use fallback
transitions.observation: Fallback is delayed until retry budget is consumed

options.result: The policy repeats a permanent error and delays the fallback without improving the chance of success.
options.explanation: Retry only errors likely to change on a subsequent attempt. Authentication and schema errors usually need correction, not repetition.

options.label: Retry transient errors; fail over on permanent errors
options.context: Timeouts get one jittered retry. Invalid credentials are surfaced and the known-good fallback is available.

predictions.label: Transient errors get a capped retry; permanent errors stop early
Stop after the first error without fallback

transitions.label: Classify provider response
transitions.observation: Timeout is transient; invalid credentials are permanent

transitions.label: Handle timeout
transitions.observation: One retry is allowed; if still unavailable, use fallback

transitions.label: Handle invalid credential
transitions.observation: Do not retry; alert operator and return safe fallback

options.result: Transient failures get a bounded retry; permanent failures stop, alert, and use the safe fallback.
options.explanation: Retries need a deadline, jitter, and idempotent effects. A fallback must preserve its source and uncertainty; never claim a provider call succeeded when it did not.

options.label: Stop after the first provider error
options.context: No retry and no cached response are configured.

predictions.label: Transient errors get a capped retry; permanent errors stop early
Stop after the first error without fallback

transitions.label: Return status
transitions.observation: Request is unavailable; no unsupported answer is emitted

options.result: The service fails clearly and safely, but gives up even when a bounded retry could recover.
options.explanation: Failing closed avoids invented output, but availability may suffer. A production policy balances a bounded retry and truthful degradation against latency and duplicate side effects.

ai-39.title: Readiness review: evidence beats a green dashboard
ai-39.prompt: A launch review finds healthy aggregate metrics, but the on-call engineer has not practiced rollback and the alert has no named owner. Choose a readiness policy and predict the launch decision.
ai-39.controlPrompt: What evidence is required before launch?
ai-39.predictionPrompt: Should launch proceed with the evidence currently available?

options.label: Launch when aggregate dashboard is green
options.context: Current health metrics are green; operational ownership is not checked.

transitions.label: Check alert ownership
transitions.observation: No named responder · unchecked by this policy

transitions.label: Launch
transitions.observation: Release proceeds without practiced response evidence

options.result: The dashboard-only policy launches despite missing operational ownership and rollback evidence.
options.explanation: Service health is only one part of readiness. Teams also need an owner, a tested rollback, meaningful alerts, and a runbook that an unfamiliar operator can use.

options.label: Require named ownership and a practiced rollback
options.context: A launch gate checks an alert owner, runbook, and a successful rollback exercise.

transitions.label: Check operator evidence
transitions.observation: No named responder and rollback drill missing

transitions.label: Hold launch
transitions.observation: Assign an owner and practice recovery before release

options.result: Launch is held until an operator can respond and the rollback path is demonstrated.
options.explanation: Readiness criteria should be concrete and verifiable. A checklist is not complete merely because every box is marked; retain the evidence, owner, and date.

options.label: Accept missing controls with a documented exception
options.context: A named risk owner may approve a time-limited exception with a mitigation and expiry.

transitions.label: Check risk exception
transitions.observation: No named risk owner or expiry recorded

transitions.label: Hold launch
transitions.observation: No valid exception exists; record owner and expiry first

options.result: No exception is valid until an accountable owner accepts the risk and records an expiry.
options.explanation: Risk acceptance is a governance decision, not a way to erase a failed control. A valid exception states the impact, mitigation, owner, and expiry.

ai-40.title: Capstone architecture: trace one request across boundaries
ai-40.prompt: A document assistant must answer with evidence, survive a worker restart, and avoid repeating side effects. Choose an architecture and predict the state after a crash immediately following document retrieval.
ai-40.controlPrompt: How should the request and its effects be coordinated?
ai-40.predictionPrompt: After the worker restarts, what state can the system safely recover?

options.label: Keep state only in an in-memory agent loop
options.context: The process has no durable checkpoint or idempotency record.

predictions.label: Restart from the beginning and risk duplicate work
Return a verified answer without rechecking

transitions.label: Retrieve documents
transitions.observation: Evidence is held only in process memory

transitions.label: Worker crashes
transitions.observation: Memory and current step are lost

transitions.label: New worker starts
transitions.observation: No checkpoint exists; workflow starts over

options.result: The request restarts without knowing which work or side effects already occurred.
options.explanation: An in-memory loop is simple, but it cannot resume safely after process loss. Any repeated external effect needs an idempotency strategy.

options.label: Persist bounded state and idempotent step results
options.context: Each step has a deadline, a durable checkpoint, an evidence reference, and a stable idempotency key.

predictions.label: Restart from the beginning and risk duplicate work
Return a verified answer without rechecking

transitions.label: Retrieve documents
transitions.observation: Store evidence references and retrieval version

transitions.label: Commit workflow checkpoint
transitions.observation: Step state and idempotency key are durable

transitions.label: Crash and resume
transitions.observation: New worker loads checkpoint and continues with the saved evidence

options.result: The request resumes from the saved retrieval checkpoint; downstream effects retain the same idempotency key.
options.explanation: Durable state enables recovery only when checkpoint writes are atomic, side effects are idempotent or deduplicated, and the evidence version remains inspectable.

options.label: Use one stateless provider request per user turn
options.context: The provider call is stateless, but this workflow requires retrieval and a later external write.

predictions.label: Restart from the beginning and risk duplicate work
Return a verified answer without rechecking

transitions.label: Retrieve documents
transitions.observation: Retrieval result is not saved with the request

transitions.label: Worker crashes
transitions.observation: No workflow state survives process loss

transitions.label: New worker starts
transitions.observation: The full operation must run again; write deduplication is still required

options.result: The request starts over because no workflow checkpoint or effect record exists.
options.explanation: A stateless call can be right for a single-turn task. Multi-step work with interruption or external effects needs a state owner, retry policy, and recovery contract.
